case_study_insert.main_stem: Zephyr Transport Routes (ZTR) is a private limited company in the road freight and logistics sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2011 by Ravi Patel, the business moves palletised goods for manufacturers and operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. ZTR plans to invest $720,000 in an automated freight-sorting hub, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $270,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $300,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $18.00, and currently handles 68,000 units a year. ZTR faces two operational problems: driver absenteeism has reached 8% and delivery defects are rising, with damaged consignments attracting complaints from manufacturing clients.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q4 2025: The sorting hub handled 17,200 consignments last quarter at a damage/defect rate of 2.4%, down from 4.1% a year earlier. Customer complaints fell from 44 to 26 per month. Average delivery time is 2.8 days. A survey of 500 manufacturing clients found that 71% would pay up to $0.50 more for guaranteed undamaged deliveries, and 58% rate on-time reliability as their top criterion. A training needs analysis shows 18 of 50 drivers have not completed on-the-job training on the new sorting systems; off-the-job training at the local college costs $750 per driver.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Zephyr Transport Routes for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.00%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% from $13.00 to $13.72 per hour from April 2026, increasing wage bills across the transport sector. (3) Diesel and energy input costs have risen 9.5% year-on-year, road-freight inflation is 6.2%, and manufacturing output grew just 1.4%, limiting the volume of goods available to haul.

questions.question_text: ZTR plans to fund part of its $720,000 sorting hub with $270,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for ZTR of using retained profit instead of increasing its $450,000 bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest charge or capital repayment, so using the $270,000 protects ZTR's cash flow at a time when it already services a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and faces fixed costs of $300,000 a year. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 9.5% rise in diesel and energy costs, helping ZTR hold its $18.00 selling price while competitors face the same input shock.

Point 2: Retaining profit avoids the additional collateral and the risk of repossession of the new automated sorting hub if demand disappoints, and it preserves Ravi Patel's control of a private limited company. No external lender can impose conditions on how the $720,000 investment is run, so management keeps full freedom to reorganise the hierarchical structure and tackle the 8% driver absenteeism without interference from a bank keen to protect its own lending. With revenue of $2,400,000 in 2024 and gross profit of $960,000 shown in Appendix 2, ZTR has a sufficient internal profit base to release $270,000 without endangering working cash.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to ZTR and its sorting-hub financing decision.

questions.question_text: ZTR is launching its guaranteed undamaged delivery service. Consider a national television campaign, regional radio sponsorship, or targeted social media advertising. Which should ZTR choose to promote the service? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Television campaign: A national TV campaign would build rapid, broad awareness of the guaranteed undamaged service across all manufacturing clients, but airtime and production costs are very high and most viewers are not commercial freight buyers. For a 50-employee firm funding a $720,000 hub and a $450,000 loan, the wastage of spend would be severe and the message would reach very few of the 500 surveyed clients.

Regional radio sponsorship: Radio is much cheaper and can target the industrial corridors ZTR serves, reinforcing reliability messages to local logistics managers. However, its reach is narrow and cannot support a national reputation for undamaged deliveries; the 58% of surveyed clients who rank on-time reliability first are spread far beyond any one radio region.

Social media advertising: Targeted online ads can reach exactly the 71% of 500 surveyed clients willing to pay $0.50 more for guaranteed undamaged deliveries, with measurable engagement and precise geographic and industry targeting at low cost. Results build more slowly than TV, but the $0.50 premium and reliability message can be demonstrated directly to procurement decision-makers.

Recommendation: ZTR should choose targeted social media advertising. It reaches the precise segment identified in the survey, costs far less than television, and scales nationally unlike radio. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a firm with a $450,000 loan; radio is rejected as too narrow for a national freight reputation, though small regional tests could supplement the digital campaign once results are measured. The 2.8-day average delivery time can also be showcased in the adverts to make the reliability claim concrete.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of ZTR with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of ZTR with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: ZTR's driver absenteeism has reached 8% and its hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership is unpopular. Explain two benefits for ZTR of introducing democratic leadership to improve motivation among its drivers.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives ZTR's workforce of 50 a genuine voice in how the new automated sorting hub is organised, helping satisfy social and esteem needs and raising job satisfaction. Drivers who help design delivery rounds and shift patterns are more likely to attend consistently, directly reducing the 8% absenteeism that currently disrupts the 68,000-unit operation and strains the $450,000 loan commitment.

Point 2: Consulting drivers generates practical ideas for reducing the rising delivery defects and damaged consignments, since they handle the freight daily. Greater involvement raises commitment and lowers labour turnover, saving the $750 per driver external training cost and protecting service quality while the $720,000 sorting hub is introduced. Higher morale also supports the on-time reliability that 58% of manufacturing clients rank as their top buying criterion, strengthening ZTR's position when tendering for new contracts. The 2.4% defect rate has already fallen from 4.1%, showing that engaged staff can improve quality, and democratic leadership builds on that momentum while the hierarchical structure is adjusted.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ZTR's absenteeism, quality and output.

questions.question_text: ZTR must train 18 drivers to use the new automated sorting-hub procedures. Consider on-the-job training at the depot or off-the-job training at the local college. Which should ZTR choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training at the depot is directly relevant to ZTR's own sorting procedures and delivery routes, costs no course fees, and keeps the 18 drivers productive while they learn, protecting the 68,000-unit operation and the drive to cut the 2.4% defect rate. However, trainers are working drivers whose own deliveries suffer, bad habits can spread, and there is no formal certificate, which may matter if manufacturing clients audit quality standards.

Off-the-job training: A college course at $750 per driver gives structured, up-to-date skills and a recognised certificate for all 18, costing $13,500 in total — modest against the $720,000 hub investment. It removes drivers from the road, cutting short-term capacity, and generic content may not match ZTR's exact sorting routines, so follow-up coaching at the depot would still be needed.

Decision: ZTR should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, backed by short college sessions for senior drivers. It is cheapest, depot-specific and avoids further capacity loss while absenteeism is already 8%; full off-the-job training is rejected because paying $13,500 and releasing 18 drivers would disrupt the delivery schedule, and college visits can be added once the sorting hub stabilises and the 2.4% defect rate is under control. With 17,200 consignments handled last quarter, even a short loss of depot capacity would delay deliveries to the 500 manufacturing clients. On-the-job training avoids that risk entirely, and the $13,500 saved can fund refresher sessions later if the 2.4% defect rate does not improve. Senior drivers can then cascade these skills to the rest of the workforce, extending the benefit of the $720,000 hub investment across the depot.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to ZTR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of ZTR.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of ZTR with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how ZTR's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $300,000 ÷ ($18.00 − $12.00) = $300,000 ÷ $6.00 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $18.00 − $12.00 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways ZTR's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 50,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 68,000 units shows a margin of safety of 18,000 units, confirming the freight operation is profitable and guiding whether to commit to the $720,000 sorting hub.
2. Contribution per unit of $6.00 lets managers model a discount: the $0.50 premium identified in the client survey, if given as a price concession, would cut contribution to $5.50 and push break-even up to about 54,545 units ($300,000 ÷ $5.50), so extra volume must justify it.
3. With fixed costs of $300,000, managers can set the volume needed to service the $450,000 bank loan and check that 68,000 units is sufficient before the company borrows further.
4. Unit cost data ($300,000 ÷ 68,000 units + $12.00 = $16.41 a unit) can be benchmarked each quarter to detect the rising delivery defects and damaged consignments, and to judge whether the 9.5% energy-cost rise is being absorbed.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 50,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 18,000 units against 68,000 output; discount modelling with $0.50 and $5.50 contribution; loan servicing against $300,000 fixed costs; and unit-cost benchmarking at $16.41 to tackle delivery defects.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate the profitability of ZTR by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and return on capital employed (ROCE) for 2024 and 2025. Has ZTR's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.5%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 20.0%
ROCE 2025 = 24.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $960,000 on revenue of $2,400,000 compares with 2025 gross profit of $1,260,000 on revenue of $2,800,000; cost of sales rose only from $1,440,000 to $1,540,000 while revenue grew faster. Operating profit increased from $300,000 to $420,000, and capital employed from $1,500,000 to $1,750,000; interest payable rose from $30,000 to $45,000 but remains small.

Evaluation: Every measure points the same way. The 40.0% to 45.0% move shows ZTR kept more of each revenue dollar after direct freight costs, so the 9.5% diesel and energy shock was at least partly passed on through the $18.00 selling price. The 12.5% to 15.0% operating result shows better control of overheads relative to revenue, and the 20.0% to 24.0% return on capital employed indicates the existing asset base is generating more operating profit even as the $720,000 sorting hub is being funded. Interest payable remains modest, so the $450,000 loan is not yet a heavy burden. The main caution is that capital employed grew faster than revenue, so future returns depend on the hub winning enough consignments.

Conclusion: ZTR's financial performance has clearly improved. Gross margin, operating margin and return on capital employed all rose together between 2024 and 2025, and the improvement is broad-based rather than driven by a one-off. ZTR should proceed with the $720,000 investment while monitoring that the new capital earns comparable returns.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates all three profitability ratios for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of margins, operating profit and capital employed and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for ZTR of introducing a guaranteed undamaged delivery service for its manufacturing clients.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The client survey found 71% of 500 manufacturers would pay up to $0.50 more for guaranteed undamaged deliveries, so ZTR can add a premium that protects its $6.00 contribution per unit even as diesel and energy costs rise 9.5%. It also matches the 58% of clients who rank on-time reliability first, strengthening ZTR's chance of winning contracts for the new $720,000 sorting hub.

Disadvantage: Guaranteeing no damage requires better packing, careful handling and inspection, which would raise the $12.00 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins unless the full $0.50 premium is accepted across all 68,000 units. Any failure would trigger compensation claims and damage the reputation ZTR is trying to build, and the current 2.4% defect rate shows damage is not yet eliminated. With a $450,000 loan to service, ZTR has limited room to absorb a costly guarantee that clients may demand without paying extra. The 8% absenteeism also makes consistently undamaged, on-time service harder to guarantee.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to ZTR's survey data, costs and investment.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.00%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 9.5% rise in diesel and energy input costs will affect ZTR. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 5.00%): If ZTR's $450,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $450,000 = $3,375 a year (0.0075 × $450,000). That is small beside fixed costs of $300,000, and if the loan is fixed-rate the increase is zero. Higher rates may also make clients cautious and raise the cost of any future borrowing, but ZTR can largely neutralise this by fixing the loan rate.

Minimum wage increase (5.5%, to $13.72 per hour): ZTR employs a workforce of 50, many in driving and handling roles, so a wage rise feeds into its cost base and is not optional. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay, so no defensible annual wage total can be invented; the honest test is productivity — 68,000 units ÷ 50 staff = 1,360 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is affordable; if absenteeism at 8% lowers it, unit labour cost rises and the $6.00 contribution per unit is squeezed.

Diesel and energy inputs (9.5%): ZTR's variable cost of $12.00 per unit will be affected, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 9.5% it would add 9.5% × $12.00 = $1.14 per unit, and at 68,000 units that is about $77,500 a year (68,000 × $1.14). Even a smaller pass-through cuts the $6.00 contribution materially. ZTR can offset part through the $0.50 undamaged-delivery premium found in the survey.

Conclusion: The 9.5% diesel and energy rise will have the greatest impact because it compounds across all 68,000 consignments and directly erodes the $6.00 contribution that justifies the $720,000 hub. The wage rise is second because it can be managed through productivity; the interest-rate effect is smallest and can be fixed. ZTR should pursue the $0.50 premium and fuel-efficient routing to protect its margins.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to ZTR.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on ZTR's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of ZTR with a well-justified judgment that energy costs have the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
